name: Ad hominem
definition: Attacking a person instead of assessing the argument.
argument: We can ignore her transit proposal because she is an unpleasant person.
weakness: Character does not resolve the proposal’s costs or benefits.
refutation: Separate the speaker from the claim. Ask for evidence about the proposal.

name: Straw man
definition: Replacing an opponent’s claim with a weaker version.
argument: You support one car-free street, so you want to ban every car in the city.
weakness: One car-free street is not a universal ban.
refutation: Restate the original scope and assess that specific proposal.

name: False dilemma
definition: Presenting two options when plausible alternatives exist.
argument: Either we cancel the program entirely or we accept every part of it unchanged.
weakness: Revision, a pilot, or partial adoption are possible alternatives.
refutation: Name an omitted option and compare it using the same criteria.

name: Hasty generalization
definition: Drawing a broad conclusion from insufficient evidence.
argument: Two people disliked the workshop; therefore, workshops never help anyone.
weakness: Two reports cannot support a universal claim.
refutation: Ask how the sample was selected and what the broader outcomes show.

name: Post hoc
definition: Inferring causation from temporal sequence alone.
argument: Productivity fell after we changed the logo, so the new logo caused the decline.
weakness: Sequence alone does not establish a causal connection.
refutation: Identify other changes and propose a comparison that tests the cause.

name: Circular reasoning
definition: Using the conclusion as support for itself.
argument: This policy is the best because no other policy is better.
weakness: The premise repeats the conclusion without independent support.
refutation: Request an external criterion and evidence against that criterion.

name: Appeal to popularity
definition: Treating widespread belief as proof of truth.
argument: Most people believe the claim, so it must be true.
refutation: Ask for independent evidence while acknowledging the popularity.

name: Slippery slope
definition: Assuming a chain of escalating effects without enough support.
argument: If we extend one deadline, soon nobody will ever finish any work.
weakness: The predicted escalation needs a mechanism and supporting evidence.
refutation: Test each causal link and consider limits on the exception.

name: Equivocation
definition: Changing the meaning of a key word within an argument.
argument: The brochure says the service is free. Free people have no restrictions, so this service cannot have any rules.
weakness: Free of charge and free of restrictions are different meanings.
refutation: Define the term consistently and reassess the inference.

name: Red herring
definition: Introducing an irrelevant issue to distract from the question.
argument: Why discuss the failed safety inspection when our office has won a design award?
weakness: The design award does not answer the safety question.
refutation: Acknowledge the separate topic and return to inspection evidence.

name: Appeal to ignorance
definition: Treating a lack of disproof as proof.
argument: Nobody has proved this device does not work, so it definitely works.
weakness: The absence of disproof does not establish effectiveness.
refutation: Request a positive test with a clear success criterion.

name: Tu quoque
definition: Dismissing a criticism because the critic is inconsistent.
argument: You also arrive late, so your argument that punctuality matters is false.
weakness: The critic’s inconsistency does not establish that the principle is false.
refutation: Separate the standard’s merit from whether either person meets it.
